The next, his knife struck a deep gouge into scenery instead of survivors — every mistimed impact punished with a jolt from the cuff that lit up the room. Sparks spat from the device with every failure, stinging the air with ozone. The world reeked of metal and heat and something burning beneath the skin. Inside his head, the betrayal was worse than the pain. His body had never refused him before, not since he carved himself into something more than human. Now every strike mocked him. He could feel their eyes watching, registering each misfire. Prey saw his weakness. He would rather have died on the spot than endure it. The survivors, though, didn’t see weakness. They saw something worse. An apex predator had rhythm: chase, lunge, recover. Predictable in its terror. But this? This was coin-flip chaos. Every time he rounded a corner, they didn’t know if he’d miss them entirely or strike so hard their bones would powder. Claudette pressed flat against a pallet, tears leaking silent as she watched the red flare at his wrist. Nea crept around a corridor edge, hood half off, staring at the sparks instead of his eyes. Gabriel crouched low near a half-finished gen, studying the erratic stutter of Wesker’s movements. They didn’t seem so random now that he was watching closely. They couldn’t look away. And they couldn’t linger. Because Wesker’s thrashing was still deadly, every jolt turning him more into a thrashing weapon. Pallets shattered under blows meant for flesh, walls cracked from impacts that should have been clean grapples. Metal walls dented where his fists drove too far. His voice was a storm, every snarl bouncing down the halls like a wild animal caught in a cage too small. There was no rhythm to dodge, no pattern to learn. Just violence, jagged and wrong. The survivors couldn’t get close — every angle dissolved into chaos before they could lock their eyes on what they needed. They fled because to stand too near was to risk being crushed by sheer chaotic force. They weren’t running from Wesker. They were running from a bomb. By the time the final gen sparked alive, the trial looked like a war zone. Steve limped through a hole in the wall that hadn’t existed when the match began. Nea had a cut on her forehead from a ricocheted board. Claudette’s fingers trembled as she reset a bandage that had soaked through mid-match. Gabriel hadn’t touched a gen. He spent the whole match watching, dodging, calculating, and still came back with a split eyebrow and a gouged side. At the gate, no one spoke. They didn’t need to. Even Gabriel looked shaken. Back at the fire, the warmth barely reached them. Claudette sat closest, her arms wrapped tight around herself. “Those sparks...” Her voice cracked. “They weren’t random. Every time he froze, every time he twitched, it lit up.” Nea shoved her hood back, hair sticking damp to her temple. “And the sound. You heard it, right? Like something shorting out. Circuits frying. I’ve built enough rigs to know.” Jake barked a laugh, but it was hollow. “So what? He’s frying alive, big deal. Easier for us.” But he wouldn’t meet anyone’s eyes. “That’s not the point, Jake!” Claudette snapped, sharper than usual. “It’s not some coincidence he’s losing trials! That band is clearly driving him insane.” Meg laughed — too loud. “Oh, come on. A conspiracy now? What, he’s got a car battery under his coat for the sparking effect? He’s just slipping. End of story.” But her bravado cracked as her voice pitched too high. She looked away, jaw clenched. Gabriel settled onto a log, fresh wrappings over his side already seeping through. He rested his elbows on his knees, eyes on the fire. His voice was calm. Measured. “I couldn’t get close enough to really see,” he said. “But it’s definitely hardware. And if it’s hardware...” He lifted his gaze, scanning the circle. “...then someone’s using it.” The fire popped. No one laughed. No one argued. Even the pragmatists shifted, restless. The image of Wesker tearing through the trial like a cornered animal — sparks flying, screams echoing, walls coming down around him — clung to them all. The Fog hadn’t just unbalanced him. It had weaponized his suffering. Later, when the others had drifted into uneasy silence or disappeared into the tents, Gabriel stayed by the fire — gaze distant, mind still racing. He hadn’t seen it close enough. How was it situated? Could he get it off? He needed a closer look, but there was only one way to get it. Next time... he’d let Wesker grab him. Not for long. Just long enough. He had to know. Chapter 10 – Residue The reset came, but it didn’t bring peace. Wesker dropped to the floor of the station like a severed cable, his body refusing to respond with anything resembling precision. For a moment he stayed there — not by choice, but because his limbs simply wouldn't move. He tried to rise. Failed the first time. Vision swam. His stomach lurched. Knees crumpled. A palm caught the wall — and left a smear of red where it dragged down the paneling. That shouldn't still be there. The Fog was supposed to take these things — blood, sweat, breath. Pain. That was the contract. The pattern. The law. But lately... the Fog was leaving things behind. His body still heaved with the last trial’s ruin. Every breath dragged as if through smoke. His chest spasmed mid-inhale, ribs jerking under phantom pressure. Something hot clung to his spine like oil. His fingers trembled. Muscles flinched from old burns that should’ve never made it past the gate. The cuff at his wrist didn’t hum. Didn’t burn. Just sat there — quiet now. Patient.
